newsitem.title: KENYA: FOCUS-Kenya shilling falls pending IMF loan talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kenya shilling falls pending IMF loan talks.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling took a severe beating on Thursday as the currency markets nervously awaited an International Monetary Fund (IMF) decision on loans to prop up the economy of the embattled east African nation.

Dealers said the market traded nervously as anxiety-gripped foreign investors and business managers awaited the make or break IMF verdict. An announcement was expected in Washington later on Thursday or early on Friday.
The shilling weakened sharply against the dollar, losing around 86 cents to trade at a mean commercial rate of 58.92 compared with Wednesday's 58.06 close.
And it took an even harder battering from sterling, losing 1.91 shillings to trade at 96.6.
Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi denied reports that talks with the IMF, largely over graft concerns and implementation deadlines, had collapsed. But his comments failed to calm a nervous market.
Officials said talks between treasury and IMF officials had continued into Thursday, discussing government measures to clamp down on corruption.
"The talks have not collapsed," Mudavadi told Reuters, adding that he would give more details on the question at a news conference he has called for 1500 local time (1200 GMT).
An IMF deadline set last month for the government to prove its commitment to fight corruption and reform the energy sector expires on Thursday.

Kenya risks losing a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) loan worth $205 million which was extended in April last year. Disbursements were made conditional on Kenya meeting reform pledges.

The last scheduled ESAF payment, a $36 million tranche, was delayed by the IMF for a month from June 30 mainly because of concern at how Kenyan authorities had handled the multi-million dollar Goldenberg International financial scandal.
"The market is nervous about the disbursement of the second loan by the IMF," said a dealer.
"People are afraid foreign investors might come in and buy dollars aggressively, they are marking up prices cautiously," said another trader.
Another dealer said the impact of the IMF decision on the shilling represented a trend that had developed over the last few months.
Foreign investors were the first to flee the market, they said.
"Those guys (foreign investors) out there are not on the ground, they don't know the reality of the situation," one dealer said. "At the first sign of trouble they just want out."

But one dealer played down the importance of the IMF talks, saying that Thursday's weakening of the shilling was symptomatic of political instability in the last few weeks as the opposition cornered President Daniel arap Moi on constitutional reforms.

Nine people died in violent clashes between riot police and pro-reform demonstrators in the Kenyan capital early in July, an incident that jolted foreign investors and marred the image of east Africa's economic engine.
"It's not really the IMF that's affecting the shilling a great deal, this has been happening for a while," he said.

Dealers agreed that the prospects for the shilling were bleak over the next few weeks, cautioning that a lot would depend on how the Central Bank intervened if the IMF decided to punish Moi's discredited government.
The money market remained liquid, with overnight rates posted at between 8-15 percent.
